keyVerseText: When that year was ended, they came unto him the second year, and said unto him, We will not hide it from my lord, how that our money is spent; my lord also hath our herds of cattle; there is not ought left in the sight of my lord, but our bodies, and our lands:
rootMeaning: The root of גְּוִיָּה (gᵉvîyâh) is גֵּוָה (gêvâh), which primarily denotes the 'body' or more specifically 'the back,' implying the person as a whole. This etymology suggests that the term originally emphasized the physical, tangible aspect of a living being, focusing on the corporeal presence rather than an abstract or spiritual concept. The prolonged form גְּוִיָּה thus extends this meaning to refer explicitly to the body, whether living or dead, highlighting the physicality and mortality inherent in human existence.
usageInScripture: Throughout Scripture, גְּוִיָּה appears thirteen times and is consistently translated to denote either a living body or a corpse. The top translations such as 'and the bodies,' 'their bodies,' and 'of their corpses' reflect this dual usage, indicating that the word encompasses both the animate and inanimate state of a body. This range shows that the term is not limited to death but also includes living flesh, as seen in Genesis 47:18 and Daniel 10:6. The lexical evidence from visions and historical narratives confirms its flexibility in describing physical bodies in various states.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding גְּוִיָּה as both living body and dead corpse underscores the biblical tension between mortality and the hope of resurrection central to the Christian faith. It reminds believers that our physical bodies are real and significant, not merely vessels but integral to our identity as created beings. The term also points to the reality of death as a consequence of sin, yet by Christ's resurrection, the body is destined for redemption and glorification. Thus, גְּוִיָּה invites reflection on the sanctity of the body and the promise of bodily resurrection, affirming the holistic nature of salvation encompassing both soul and body.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 47:18, the phrase 'but our bodies, and our lands' uses גְּוִיָּה to emphasize the totality of what remains to the people after their resources are spent. The word highlights the vulnerability and dependence of the people, indicating that beyond material possessions, their very lives—their physical bodies—are all that remain. This usage conveys a profound sense of humility and surrender, reminding us that life itself is a gift from God, and even when all else is lost, the body remains under His sovereign care.
